faq_limits_a: Usage alerts tell you as you approach your included volume. On the Startup plan, additional usage is billed at $0.30 per GB, per signal, the rate shown on this page. If you would rather not go over, set an overage cap per signal and ingest for that signal is rejected at the cap.

faq_trial_a: The Startup plan starts with a 14-day free trial. A credit card is required, and you are not charged until the trial ends. Enterprise plans start with a conversation.
page_home_title: Open Source Observability for Traces, Logs & Metrics | Maple
page_home_desc: Open-source observability built on OpenTelemetry. Traces, logs, metrics and session replay in one place, with an MCP server your AI agent can query.
page_pricing_desc: One plan: $39/month with 100 GB of logs, traces and metrics each, then a flat $0.30/GB. No per-seat, per-host or per-query fees. Estimate your bill in seconds.
page_otel_desc: Maple is built on OpenTelemetry. Ingest traces, logs, and metrics over OTLP. No proprietary agents, no vendor lock-in.
page_otel_heading: Built on OpenTelemetry from the ground up
page_otel_subtitle: Maple is an OTel-native observability platform. Traces, logs, and metrics all arrive through the open standard. No proprietary agents, no SDK lock-in.
page_otel_what_is_p1: OpenTelemetry is the CNCF open-source standard for collecting observability data from distributed systems. It provides a single, vendor-neutral set of APIs, SDKs, and tools to instrument your applications and export traces, logs, and metrics.
page_otel_what_is_p2: With support for every major language and framework, OTel has become the industry default for telemetry instrumentation, backed by contributions from hundreds of organizations.
page_otel_no_vendor_desc: Your instrumentation stays the same regardless of which backend you choose. Switch providers without touching application code.
page_otel_one_standard_desc: Traces, logs, and metrics share a unified data model with correlated context. No stitching together separate tools.
page_otel_community_desc: Backed by the CNCF and hundreds of contributors. The spec is governed by the community, and no single vendor sets its roadmap.
page_otel_language_desc: Official SDKs for Go, Java, Python, JavaScript, .NET, Rust, and more. Auto-instrumentation is available for most frameworks.
page_otel_future_desc: As the industry converges on OTel, instrumentation you write today keeps working with whatever backend you use next.
page_otel_ecosystem_desc: Collectors, exporters, processors, and connectors: a pipeline you can shape to match your infrastructure.
page_otel_spec_otlp_desc: Send telemetry over OTLP/HTTP, as protobuf or JSON. No translation layers, no proprietary formats.
page_otel_spec_semantic_desc: Maple reads the OTel semantic conventions for HTTP, database, RPC, and messaging spans and builds its views from them.
page_otel_spec_signals_desc: Traces, logs, and metrics are each stored, queried, and correlated with the others.
page_otel_spec_collector_desc: Use the OpenTelemetry Collector to route, filter, and batch telemetry before sending it to Maple.
page_otel_spec_sdk_desc: Works with every official OTel SDK. If it speaks OTLP, Maple can ingest it. No vendor-specific libraries required.
page_otel_spec_context_desc: W3C Trace Context is supported. Spans and logs from different services correlate by trace ID.
page_otel_ecosystem_heading: Works with your existing OTel setup
page_otel_ecosystem_p1: Already using the OpenTelemetry Collector, auto-instrumentation agents, or OTel SDKs? Point your OTLP exporter at Maple with an ingest key. Nothing else in your pipeline changes.
page_otel_ecosystem_p2: Maple fits into the OTel ecosystem as a backend. It receives, stores, and visualizes the telemetry your existing pipeline produces. Your instrumentation stays as it is.
page_roadmap_desc: What Maple has shipped, what is in progress, and what comes next.
page_roadmap_subtitle: What's shipped, what's in progress, and what comes next.

page_k8s_correlation_desc: Go from a slow trace to the pod and node that ran it.
page_k8s_kube_state_desc: Deployments, replicas and pod status, collected by the chart. No separate kube-state-metrics needed.
page_k8s_views_desc: Four views that share the same filters, from a whole deployment down to one pod.
page_k8s_operator_desc: Pods in an annotated namespace are configured automatically. Apps with an OTel SDK need no code changes.
page_k8s_multi_desc: One endpoint for prod, staging and local clusters. Tell them apart by cluster name.

page_k8s_views_nodes_lede: Kubelet stats per node, with uptime and lifecycle.

faq_home_what_a: Maple is an observability platform for traces, logs, metrics and session replay, built on OpenTelemetry and backed by ClickHouse. It lets you collect, visualize, and query telemetry from distributed systems in real time, or let an AI agent do it for you over MCP.
faq_home_oss_a: Maple's source is on GitHub under the Functional Source License (FSL-1.1). You can read every line, fork it, and self-host. Each release becomes Apache 2.0 two years after publication. You can run Maple yourself or use the hosted version.
faq_home_otel_a: Yes. Maple is built on OpenTelemetry, the open, vendor-neutral standard for telemetry, so there are no proprietary agents. If you already emit OpenTelemetry data, you can point it at Maple without re-instrumenting your code.
faq_home_price_a: The Startup plan is $39/month with 100 GB of logs, traces, and metrics each included, then a flat $0.30 per GB. No per-host or per-seat fees. Enterprise plans add custom volume and retention.
faq_home_agents_q: Does Maple work with AI agents?
faq_home_agents_a: Yes. Maple runs an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server, so compatible AI agents can list services, search traces, find errors, and propose fixes directly against your telemetry.
hero_announce_text: Maple Local: one binary, no account.
signals_trace_sub: Every request as a span tree, attributes intact. Click a span and see what it carried.
signals_logs_sub: Structured logs straight from OTLP. Filter by severity, service, or any attribute, then jump to the trace.
signals_session_sub: Every click, route, console line, and failed request. Replay and spans share one session id.
incident_title: From a 3 AM page to the line that caused it.
incident_lede: Four surfaces, one trace id. Every step below opens from the one before it.
incident_step_1_body: Error rate on api-gateway crosses 5%. The alert carries the service, the threshold it broke and the spans that failed. Route it to Slack, Discord, Telegram, PagerDuty, email, or any webhook.
incident_step_2_title: The trace opens on the failing span.

incident_step_4_title: Or hand it to an agent.

platform_errors_desc: Errors grouped by type across every service, with trends over time, affected services, and sample traces attached.
platform_alerts_desc: Alert on error rate, latency, Apdex, throughput, any query-builder chart or raw SQL. Incidents open and resolve on their own. Routed to Slack, Discord, Telegram, PagerDuty, email, or any webhook.

hero_shot_overview_line: Health, latency and errors across your system.
hero_shot_traces_line: Follow one request end to end.
page_cta_lede: One endpoint, one key. Traces, logs, metrics and sessions, linked from the first request.
feat_tracing_seo_desc: Open one trace and read where the time went: waterfall, flamegraph and service flow over the same spans, with every attribute the SDK sent.
feat_tracing_hero_lede: A trace shows one request from start to finish. Maple keeps every span with its attributes and timing, so you can see exactly what made it slow.
feat_tracing_panel_lede: Click a span to see all its attributes, like the SQL it ran and the status it returned.
feat_tracing_cap_title: Four views of the same trace
feat_tracing_cap_1_body: Spans nested by parent and scaled to the request's length. You see the slow part before you read a number.
feat_tracing_cap_2_body: Spans stacked by depth. Fifty db.query calls in a row show up as a wall, so N+1 queries are easy to spot.
feat_tracing_cap_3_body: The trace reduced to the services it touched. Use it to find which service the time was spent in.
feat_tracing_cap_4_body: Every attribute the SDK sent, including your custom ones, is stored and searchable.
feat_tracing_cap_5_body: Open any span's logs in one click. They share the same trace id.
feat_tracing_artifact_lede: The same component the product uses. Hover a span to see its service and duration.
feat_sessions_seo_desc: Watch the session the user actually had, then open the trace behind any moment in it. Replay, console, network and spans share one session id.
feat_sessions_hero_title: Watch it happen, then open the trace
feat_sessions_hero_lede: The replay shows what the user did. The trace shows why it broke. One click takes you from one to the other.
feat_sessions_panel_title: The recording and the evidence, side by side
feat_sessions_panel_lede: Console logs, network requests and errors play back on the same timeline as the user's clicks.
feat_sessions_cap_1_body: Clicks, inputs, console logs, network calls and errors in one timeline, each linked to its trace.
feat_sessions_cap_2_body: We record the page, not a video. Scrolling, hovers and typing play back exactly, at any screen size.
feat_sessions_cap_3_title: From a moment to a span
feat_sessions_cap_3_body: Pause on a failed click and open the request it sent.
feat_sessions_cap_4_body: Every request with its method, status and duration. A failed checkout shows up the moment it happens.
feat_sessions_cap_5_body: Inputs and text are masked in the browser before anything is sent. You control sampling and masking in the SDK.

feat_logs_seo_desc: Search structured logs across every service, filter by severity and resource attribute, and open the trace that produced any line.
feat_logs_hero_title: Search logs, jump to the trace
feat_logs_hero_lede: Logs arrive structured and linked to their trace. Any result opens the request that wrote it.
feat_logs_panel_title: Filter by severity, service and attribute
feat_logs_panel_lede: Filter counts match the time range you picked, so what you see is what you get.
feat_logs_cap_title: What you can do with a log line
feat_logs_cap_1_body: Filter on service.name, environment or your own keys, just like the message text.
feat_logs_cap_2_body: Each severity level has its own color and filter. WARN and ERROR are one click apart.
feat_logs_cap_3_body: Jump from any log line to the span that was running when it was written.
feat_logs_cap_4_body: A chart above the results, colored by severity, shows an error burst before you read a line.
feat_logs_cap_5_body: Logs come in over OTLP with your traces and metrics. No extra agent or pipeline.
feat_logs_artifact_lede: New lines stream in, tagged with service and severity. Same data as search.
feat_metrics_seo_desc: Browse every metric your services emit, then build dashboards on the same data the trace list reads from, so a chart and a trace can never disagree.

feat_metrics_hero_lede: Dashboards read the same data as your traces. If a chart shows p99 at 380 ms, the traces behind it are one click away.
feat_metrics_panel_lede: See each metric's type, the service that sends it, and when it was last seen.
feat_metrics_cap_1_body: p50, p95 and p99 on one chart, in the same colors everywhere in the product.
feat_metrics_cap_2_body: One number and the line it should stay under, like error rate against its budget.
feat_metrics_cap_3_body: Add $service or $env once and every chart follows it. One dashboard instead of twelve.
feat_metrics_cap_4_body: Group-by suggests only attributes the metric really has, so charts never come up empty.
feat_metrics_cap_5_body: Select a time range on any latency chart to see the traces inside it.
feat_metrics_artifact_lede: Five hours in five-minute buckets. A single number would hide the warning spike and the errors after it.
feat_catalog_seo_desc: Every service with its latency percentiles, error rate and throughput, and a live map of who calls whom, both built from spans.
feat_catalog_hero_title: A service map that builds itself
feat_catalog_hero_lede: No setup. Maple builds the map from your traces, and new services show up the first time they're called.
feat_catalog_panel_lede: Latency, error rate and throughput per service. Sort by p99 to find the one that needs attention.
feat_catalog_cap_1_body: Every line is traffic that actually happened, with its own request and error rate.
feat_catalog_cap_2_body: Postgres, Redis and third-party APIs appear on the map next to your services.
feat_catalog_cap_3_body: Pick a service to see only what it talks to. Forty services shrink to the few that matter.
feat_catalog_cap_4_body: Each service keeps its color on the map, in traces and in charts.
feat_catalog_cap_5_body: Releases are marked on each service's latency chart, so you can see which version caused a change.
feat_catalog_artifact_lede: Each service shows its request rate, error rate and latency. Lines show traffic between them.
feat_errors_seo_desc: Exceptions grouped into issues by type and normalized message, each one linked to the span that threw it and the release that introduced it.
feat_errors_hero_lede: Maple groups the same error into one issue and links every occurrence to the span that threw it.
feat_errors_panel_lede: Each issue shows its type, affected services, count and when it was last seen.
feat_errors_cap_1_body: Errors with the same type, message and stack are one issue. Ids, hosts and emails are ignored when matching.
feat_errors_cap_2_body: Every issue opens the trace it came from, with the query and status code at the time.
feat_errors_cap_3_body: See when an issue first and last appeared. A resolved issue that comes back reopens.
feat_errors_cap_4_body: Claim an issue, set severity and leave notes, so the next person on call knows what you tried.
feat_errors_cap_5_body: New errors are grouped every minute and AI suggests a severity. Your choice always overrides it.
feat_alerts_seo_desc: Threshold alerts on traces, logs and metrics, previewed against your own history before you save, evaluated every minute, and delivered to Slack, Discord, Telegram, PagerDuty, email, or any webhook.
feat_alerts_hero_lede: Test a rule against past data before you save it. Every check is logged, so you always know why an alert fired, or didn't.
feat_alerts_panel_lede: The preview uses the same logic as the real alert, so it shows exactly when it would have fired.
feat_alerts_cap_1_body: Error rate, latency, Apdex and throughput built in. Or alert on any query over traces, logs and metrics, or raw SQL.
feat_alerts_cap_2_body: If the preview says it would have fired twice last Tuesday, it would have.
feat_alerts_cap_3_body: Group by service or any attribute, and each group alerts on its own. One bad service can't hide in an average.
feat_alerts_cap_4_body: Each check records its value and result, including failures. If a rule stays quiet, you can see why.
feat_alerts_cap_5_body: Automatic retries, custom templates and reminders while an incident is open. Slack, Discord, Telegram, PagerDuty, email, Hazel or any webhook.
feat_alerts_artifact_title: From breach to page in a minute
feat_alerts_artifact_lede: Rules run every minute. Two bad checks in a row open an incident and notify you. Two good ones close it.

feat_mcp_hero_lede: Maple's MCP server lets agents query your traces, logs and metrics, using the same queries as the dashboard.
feat_mcp_panel_lede: Connect Claude Code or any MCP client. It sees the same data you do.
feat_mcp_cap_1_body: diagnose_service reports latency, error rate and throughput, and what changed.
feat_mcp_cap_2_body: find_slow_traces and inspect_trace return real spans, so the agent sees the actual queries.
feat_mcp_cap_3_body: Link a repository and the agent can go from a stack trace to the exact line.
feat_mcp_cap_4_body: Actions that change things are separate tools. In Maple's chat, they wait for your approval.
feat_mcp_cap_5_body: Every query is locked to the org on the key. An agent can't see another team's data.
feat_mcp_artifact_lede: Five steps from list_services to propose_fix, each one a query you could run yourself.
uc_api_seo_desc: An SLO breach, traced to the release that caused it. Follow checkout p99 from the alert through the dashboard to the commit that took it from 120 ms to 380 ms.
uc_api_hero_title: The p99 moved. Find out which release moved it.
uc_api_hero_lede: An SLO is only useful if a breach points somewhere. This one goes from a threshold crossing to the commit that caused it in three surfaces, without leaving the same time range.
uc_api_story_title: Threshold to commit, in three minutes
uc_api_story_lede: One SLO holds the whole path together: checkout p99 at or under 200 ms. Every surface below is filtered to the window where it stopped being true.
uc_api_step_1_body: The rule is written against the SLO, so the notification carries the threshold, the observed value and the evaluation window. 380 ms against 200 ms, sustained across three windows.
uc_api_step_2_title: The dashboard narrows it to one endpoint
uc_api_step_2_body: p50 has not moved. p99 has. That shape means a slow tail on one route rather than a service-wide slowdown, and the route breakdown names it: POST /checkout.
uc_api_step_3_body: Split the same endpoint by service.version and the step change has an owner: p99 120 ms on abc123, 380 ms on def456. The traces under def456 carry 50 db.query spans where the earlier ones carry 3.
uc_api_outcome_line: Reverted def456 at T+9:20. p99 back under the threshold on the next evaluation window.
uc_api_cap_1_title: The alert knows its own SLO
uc_api_cap_1_body: Rules are written against a percentile and a threshold, so a firing alert already contains the comparison. Nothing has to be looked up to know how far out it is.
uc_api_cap_2_title: Version is an attribute, so it is a filter
uc_api_cap_2_body: service.version rides on every span the SDK sends. Comparing two releases is a group-by.
uc_api_cap_3_body: p99 is computed from spans that are still there. Selecting the spike on the chart opens the requests inside it, so the number and the evidence are never separate artifacts.
uc_ecom_seo_desc: Checkout failures during a flash sale, traced from the alert to the Stripe timeout and the retry-exhaustion logs behind it, one order id the whole way.
uc_ecom_hero_title: Checkout is failing. Which orders, and why.
uc_ecom_hero_lede: During a sale the question is which customers lost their basket and what stopped them. One order id carries the answer across all three surfaces.
uc_ecom_story_title: One order, from the alert to the timeout
uc_ecom_story_lede: order_8421 is a real order that failed. Every surface below is filtered to it, so nothing has to be matched up by timestamp between two tools.
uc_ecom_step_1_title: The alert fires on the checkout route only
uc_ecom_step_1_body: Error rate on POST /checkout crosses its threshold while the rest of the site holds. That scoping is the first fact: the payment path is failing while the sale traffic is fine.
uc_ecom_step_2_body: Open one failed order and the waterfall is unambiguous. Three retries sit at the bottom, red, each timing out at exactly 1.75 s, the client's own deadline.
uc_ecom_step_3_title: The logs say the pool was empty
uc_ecom_step_3_body: The lines written during those spans carry the same trace id. Retry budget exhausted, then connection pool at capacity. The timeout was a symptom of waiting for a connection.
uc_ecom_outcome_line: Pool raised and the retry budget cut to two. Checkout error rate back to baseline within one evaluation window.
uc_ecom_cap_1_body: Set order.id on the span once and it is filterable everywhere spans are: the trace list, the error issue, the log search. No separate index to maintain.
uc_ecom_cap_2_body: The Stripe call is a client span with its own duration and status, so a third-party timeout is measured rather than inferred from your own error rate.
uc_ecom_cap_3_title: Logs are joined to the span
uc_ecom_cap_3_body: The lines behind a span are reached from the span, with no text query narrowed by hand to the same minute. That is the step that usually costs the most time.
uc_micro_seo_desc: Latency doubled with no deploy in sight. Follow one release across the service map, a trace and its logs to the connection pool that ran dry two hops away.
uc_micro_hero_lede: In a distributed system the service that got slow is rarely the service that broke. The map shows which edge degraded first, and the trace shows how far the wait propagated.
uc_micro_story_title: Two hops from the symptom to the cause
uc_micro_story_lede: payment-svc@1.4.2 is the release that shipped four hours before the symptom. It holds the path together: the map, the trace and the logs are all filtered to it.
uc_micro_step_1_title: The map shows a slow edge
uc_micro_step_1_body: api-gateway is the service being paged about, but its own spans are fine. The degraded edge is two hops in: payment-svc to user-db, p95 up from 12 ms to 210 ms.
uc_micro_step_2_body: Open a slow request and the db span is almost all of it. The query itself is 4 ms; the span is 210 ms. The difference is time spent before the query ever ran.
uc_micro_step_3_body: Lines from that span read pool wait 206 ms, acquired after 3 attempts. Filter by service.version and they start at 1.4.2, which raised concurrency without raising the pool.
uc_micro_outcome_line: Pool size raised to match the new concurrency. The p95 edge latency returned to 14 ms without a rollback.
uc_micro_metric_2_label: p95 edge latency, before and after
uc_micro_cap_1_body: The map measures each caller-callee pair separately, so a dependency that degraded for one caller and not another is visible as one edge.
uc_micro_cap_2_title: A db span is wait plus work
uc_micro_cap_2_body: Because the client span wraps acquisition as well as execution, pool starvation shows up as a gap between span duration and query duration instead of hiding inside a single number.
uc_micro_cap_3_title: No deploy is still a deploy
uc_micro_cap_3_body: service.version on every span means the question changes from who deployed to what version is this span from. A four-hour-old release is as findable as a four-minute-old one.

cmp_dd_seo_title: Maple vs Datadog: an open-source Datadog alternative, compared
cmp_dd_seo_desc: Maple vs Datadog for observability: where they differ, where Datadog is ahead, and what one month costs on each at list price. Open source, OpenTelemetry-native, no per-host fees.
cmp_dd_hero_lede: Datadog is the broadest observability suite on the market, and its bill is shaped by hosts, agents and add-on products. Maple is an open-source observability platform for traces, logs and metrics that ingests OpenTelemetry directly and bills on data volume. Below: where the two differ, where Datadog is ahead, and what the same month costs on each.
cmp_dd_pricing_maple: $39 a month with 100 GB per signal included, then $0.30 per GB. Browser sessions are the only other meter: 5,000 a month included, then $0.002 each.
cmp_dd_pricing_them: Infrastructure from $15 per host, APM from $31 per host, logs $0.10 per GB ingested plus $1.70 per million indexed events at 15-day retention. Custom metrics, RUM and each add-on product are priced separately.
cmp_dd_hosts_maple: None. A hundred containers on one host or one process on a hundred hosts cost the same at equal volume.
cmp_dd_hosts_them: Infrastructure and APM are both metered per host, and containers draw down a per-host allotment.
cmp_dd_agents_maple: None. Any OpenTelemetry SDK or the OpenTelemetry Collector sends OTLP straight to Maple.
cmp_dd_agents_them: The Datadog Agent and Datadog tracing libraries. OTLP is accepted through the Agent, the Collector's Datadog exporter or direct OTLP intake, and some features need the Agent.
cmp_dd_source_maple: On GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 two years after each release.
cmp_dd_source_them: Proprietary. The Agent is open source; the platform is not.
cmp_dd_selfhost_maple: Yes. Run the whole platform on your own infrastructure, including your own ClickHouse.
cmp_dd_retention_maple: 30 days on the cloud plan, longer on Enterprise, and your call when you self-host.
cmp_dd_retention_them: Indexed logs are priced at the retention you pick, 3 to 30 days; the $1.70 list rate is the 15-day option. Each other product carries its own retention.
cmp_dd_setup_maple: Point an OTLP exporter at Maple. First traces arrive within minutes.
cmp_dd_setup_them: Roll out the Agent per host or as a DaemonSet, then enable and configure each product.
cmp_dd_ai_maple: Built-in diagnostics plus a hosted MCP server, so Claude, Cursor or any agent can query your telemetry.
cmp_dd_ai_them: Bits AI across the platform and an MCP server.
cmp_dd_synthetics_maple: Not available. Alerts evaluate real traffic only.
cmp_dd_synthetics_them: API and browser tests from managed locations, priced per ten thousand runs.
cmp_dd_products_them: Network Performance Monitoring, Cloud SIEM, Cloud Security and CI Visibility: a product for each layer, each on its own meter.
cmp_dd_integrations_maple: OpenTelemetry receivers plus a catalog of connected providers: Cloudflare, Prometheus, PlanetScale, WarpStream, Hazel and GitHub. Kubernetes and Docker are agent installs.
cmp_dd_integrations_them: More than 800 vendor-maintained integrations, many for systems that never emit OpenTelemetry.
cmp_dd_rum_maple: Session replay correlated with backend traces, web analytics from the browser SDK, and a Swift SDK.
cmp_dd_rum_them: Full RUM with funnels, heatmaps and error tracking, plus mobile RUM for iOS and Android.
cmp_dd_compliance_maple: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification in progress. Maple Cloud runs in the US or the EU (Frankfurt), and self-hosting keeps the data in your own audited environment.
cmp_dd_compliance_them: SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA and FedRAMP attestations with regional sites.
cmp_dd_mig_1_body: Services already on OpenTelemetry SDKs need no code change. Add Maple as a second OTLP exporter and ship to both backends while you compare.
cmp_dd_mig_2_title: Replace the Agent with the Collector
cmp_dd_mig_2_body: Where the Datadog Agent is the only source, run the OpenTelemetry Collector with the same receivers, host metrics, Kubernetes and file logs, and export OTLP to Maple.
cmp_dd_mig_3_body: Dashboards and monitors don't cross vendors. Maple's builder and alert rules cover the common set, and the MCP server can draft both from a description.
cmp_dd_faq_1_q: Is Maple a drop-in replacement for Datadog?
cmp_dd_faq_1_a: For traces, logs, metrics, dashboards, alerting and error tracking, yes. Maple has no Synthetics, Network Performance Monitoring or Cloud SIEM, and its integration catalog is OpenTelemetry-first rather than 800 vendor connectors. Teams that live in APM, logs and infrastructure dashboards move cleanly; teams that bought Datadog for its security or network products should keep those.
cmp_dd_faq_2_q: Does Maple support the Datadog Agent?
cmp_dd_faq_2_a: No. Maple ingests OpenTelemetry, so the Datadog Agent is replaced by the OpenTelemetry Collector, which has receivers for the same sources: host metrics, Kubernetes, Docker, file logs, Prometheus endpoints. Datadog's own tracing libraries are replaced by OpenTelemetry SDKs, which cover the same languages and frameworks.
cmp_dd_faq_3_a: Yes. Add Maple as a second exporter in the Collector and send telemetry to both backends. Verify traces, logs and alerts in Maple, then remove the Datadog exporter. Nothing about the switch requires a deploy of your services if they already speak OpenTelemetry.
cmp_dd_faq_4_q: How does the pricing actually compare?
cmp_dd_faq_4_a: Maple charges $39 a month with 100 GB each of logs, traces and metrics included, then $0.30 per GB. Datadog charges per host for infrastructure and APM, per GB ingested and per million indexed events for logs, and separately for custom metrics and each add-on product. The receipts above price one reference month on both; the calculator under them prices yours.
cmp_dd_faq_5_a: Yes. The source is on GitHub under FSL-1.1 and converts to Apache 2.0 two years after each release. Run it on your own infrastructure for data residency, keep retention as long as you like, and pay for compute and storage instead of per-GB fees. The hosted cloud is there when you'd rather not operate it.
cmp_gf_seo_title: Maple vs Grafana: one platform instead of Loki, Tempo and Mimir
cmp_gf_seo_desc: Maple vs Grafana Cloud and the LGTM stack: where they differ, where Grafana is ahead, and what one month costs on each at list price. One store for traces, logs and metrics, no PromQL, LogQL or TraceQL.
cmp_gf_hero_lede: Grafana is the dashboard most engineers already know, and behind it sits a stack: Loki for logs, Tempo for traces, Mimir or Prometheus for metrics, each with its own query language. Maple is an open-source observability platform that stores all three signals in one place behind one query surface. Below: where the two differ, where Grafana is ahead, and what the same month costs on each.
cmp_gf_backends_maple: One system. Traces, logs and metrics land in one store, keyed by the same trace id.
cmp_gf_backends_them: Loki, Tempo and Mimir or Prometheus, each deployed, scaled and upgraded on its own, with Grafana in front.
cmp_gf_query_maple: One visual builder across every signal, SQL through the API and the MCP server when you want it.
cmp_gf_query_them: PromQL for metrics, LogQL for logs, TraceQL for traces.
cmp_gf_pricing_maple: $39 a month with 100 GB per signal included, then $0.30 per GB. No per-user fee.
cmp_gf_pricing_them: Free tier, then $19 a month plus $8 per active user, $6.50 per thousand active metric series, and $0.55 per GB of logs and traces: $0.05 to process, $0.40 to write and $0.10 to retain for the 30 days.
cmp_gf_seats_maple: Unlimited. Every engineer, on-call responder and manager gets a login.
cmp_gf_seats_them: $8 per active user beyond the three included on Pro.
cmp_gf_setup_maple: Point an OTLP exporter at Maple. First traces arrive within minutes.
cmp_gf_setup_them: Provision each backend, connect each as a data source, then build the first dashboard.
cmp_gf_source_maple: On GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 two years after each release. One repository for the whole platform.
cmp_gf_source_them: AGPL-3.0 for Grafana, Loki, Tempo and Mimir. Grafana Cloud itself is proprietary.
cmp_gf_selfhost_maple: One deployment: the platform and its database.
cmp_gf_selfhost_them: Self-hostable with mature Helm charts, at the cost of operating four services.
cmp_gf_otel_maple: OTLP in. Nothing else to translate.
cmp_gf_otel_them: OTLP through Alloy or the Collector, fanned out to Tempo, Loki and Mimir.
cmp_gf_plugins_maple: No plugin system. Dashboards are built from Maple's own panels.
cmp_gf_plugins_them: Hundreds of panel and data-source plugins, dashboards-as-code, and a community library of dashboards for almost anything.
cmp_gf_promql_maple: No PromQL. Existing Grafana dashboards and Prometheus alert rules don't import.
cmp_gf_promql_them: PromQL is the lingua franca. Existing dashboards and recording rules carry over unchanged.
cmp_gf_datasources_them: Query Postgres, Elasticsearch, CloudWatch and dozens more from one panel.
cmp_gf_oncall_maple: Alerts route to Slack, PagerDuty, Discord, Telegram, email and webhooks. No built-in schedules.
cmp_gf_oncall_them: Grafana IRM with on-call schedules, escalation chains and incident timelines.
cmp_gf_mig_1_body: If Alloy or the OpenTelemetry Collector already feeds Tempo, Loki and Mimir, add an OTLP exporter to Maple and run both until the alerts you care about fire from Maple.
cmp_gf_mig_2_body: Grafana JSON doesn't import. Most teams find a handful of dashboards carry the load; rebuild those in Maple's builder and let the long tail lapse.
cmp_gf_mig_3_body: Turn off Loki, Tempo, Mimir and Grafana once Maple is the source of truth. That is four services fewer to upgrade, scale and page on.
cmp_gf_faq_1_q: Does Maple replace the whole Grafana stack?
cmp_gf_faq_1_a: Yes. Maple replaces Grafana for dashboards and alerting, Loki for logs, Tempo for traces and Mimir or Prometheus for metrics with one platform. What it doesn't replace is Grafana as a general-purpose charting tool for non-telemetry data sources.
cmp_gf_faq_2_q: How is Maple different from Grafana Cloud?
cmp_gf_faq_2_a: Grafana Cloud operates Loki, Tempo and Mimir for you, but you still query three stores in three languages and pay per active user. Maple stores every signal in one place, correlates them by trace id, and has no per-user line.
cmp_gf_faq_3_q: Do I need to learn a new query language?
cmp_gf_faq_3_a: No. Maple's query builder works the same way for traces, logs and metrics. SQL is available through the API and the MCP server for the questions a builder can't express. There is no PromQL, LogQL or TraceQL to learn, and also no PromQL compatibility for dashboards you already have.
cmp_gf_faq_4_a: Yes. Maple is on GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0. The difference from the LGTM stack is that you deploy one platform and one database instead of four services with their own scaling models.
cmp_gf_faq_5_a: Maple has no plugin ecosystem. If your dashboards lean on community panels or on querying business databases alongside telemetry, Grafana is ahead here and this page says so above. Most observability dashboards use a dozen panel types, and Maple's builder covers those.
cmp_nr_seo_title: Maple vs New Relic: full-stack observability without per-user pricing
cmp_nr_seo_desc: Maple vs New Relic: where they differ, where New Relic is ahead, and what one month costs on each at list price. OpenTelemetry-native, no per-user fees, open source and self-hostable.
cmp_nr_hero_lede: New Relic is a full-stack platform priced per full-platform user plus data. Maple is an open-source observability platform for traces, logs and metrics that ingests OpenTelemetry directly and charges for data volume. Below: where the two differ, where New Relic is ahead, and what the same month costs on each.
cmp_nr_seats_maple: Unlimited. Every engineer, on-call responder and manager gets a login.
cmp_nr_seats_them: Standard: $10 for the first full-platform user, then $99 each, capped at five. Pro: $349 per user per month on an annual commitment.
cmp_nr_pricing_maple: $39 a month with 100 GB per signal included, then $0.30 per GB.

cmp_nr_agents_maple: None. OpenTelemetry SDKs and the OpenTelemetry Collector.
cmp_nr_agents_them: New Relic agents per language. OTLP is accepted, with some features available only through the agents.

cmp_nr_selfhost_maple: Yes. Run it on your own infrastructure.
cmp_nr_retention_maple: 30 days on the cloud plan, longer on Enterprise, and your call when you self-host.
cmp_nr_retention_them: Eight days for traces and 30 for logs by default. Data Plus adds up to 90 days on most data types.
cmp_nr_ai_maple: Built-in diagnostics plus a hosted MCP server, so Claude, Cursor or any agent can query your telemetry.
cmp_nr_ai_them: New Relic AI and an MCP server.
cmp_nr_synthetics_maple: Not available. Alerts evaluate real traffic only.
cmp_nr_synthetics_them: Scripted browser and API checks from managed locations, included in the platform.
cmp_nr_rum_maple: Session replay tied to backend traces, web analytics from the browser SDK, and a Swift SDK.
cmp_nr_rum_them: Browser RUM with funnels and session traces, plus mobile agents for iOS and Android.
cmp_nr_integrations_maple: OpenTelemetry receivers plus a catalog of connected providers: Cloudflare, Prometheus, PlanetScale, WarpStream, Hazel and GitHub. Kubernetes and Docker are agent installs.
cmp_nr_integrations_them: Hundreds of quickstarts and agents, including legacy runtimes without OpenTelemetry support.
cmp_nr_security_them: Vulnerability management and IAST bundled into the platform.
cmp_nr_mig_1_body: Replace New Relic's language agents with OpenTelemetry SDKs. Auto-instrumentation covers the same frameworks, and the result is portable to any backend.
cmp_nr_mig_2_body: Point the Collector or the SDK exporter at Maple alongside New Relic's OTLP endpoint. Verify traces, logs and alerts in Maple before cutting over.
cmp_nr_mig_3_body: NRQL dashboards don't import. Rebuild the ones that matter in Maple's builder and map alert policies to alert rules; the MCP server can draft both.
cmp_nr_faq_1_q: Is Maple a full replacement for New Relic?
cmp_nr_faq_1_a: For APM, logs, metrics, dashboards, alerting and error tracking, yes. For browser visibility Maple offers session replay correlated with backend traces rather than full RUM, and it has no Synthetics or vulnerability management. If those products are why you bought New Relic, keep it for them.
cmp_nr_faq_2_q: How much does the per-user pricing matter?
cmp_nr_faq_2_a: It is the largest line on the receipts above. New Relic charges per full-platform user, capped at five on Standard and $349 each on Pro. Maple has no per-user line, so the gap grows with every engineer who needs access. The receipts show it on a ten-person team.
cmp_nr_faq_3_q: Does Maple have a query language like NRQL?
cmp_nr_faq_3_a: Maple ships a visual query builder that works the same way across traces, logs and metrics, and exposes SQL through the API and the MCP server for questions the builder can't express. There is no proprietary grammar to learn.
cmp_nr_faq_4_q: Can I run both during migration?
cmp_nr_faq_4_a: Yes. Configure the OpenTelemetry Collector to export to both New Relic and Maple. Verify in Maple, then remove the New Relic exporter.
cmp_nr_faq_5_q: Is Maple open source? Can I self-host it?
cmp_nr_faq_5_a: Yes to both. The source is on GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 two years after each release. Self-host for data residency and unlimited retention, or use the hosted cloud at app.maple.dev.
cmp_d0_seo_title: Maple vs Dash0: OpenTelemetry-native observability you can self-host
cmp_d0_seo_desc: Maple vs Dash0: both OpenTelemetry-native with usage-based pricing and no per-seat fees for observability. The difference is ownership. Where they differ, where Dash0 is ahead, and what one month costs on each.
cmp_d0_hero_lede: Dash0 and Maple start from the same place: OpenTelemetry in, usage-based pricing, no per-seat fees for observability, an MCP server for agents. The difference is ownership. Maple is an open-source observability platform you can self-host; Dash0 is a closed SaaS. Below: the handful of places they differ, where Dash0 is ahead, and what the same month costs on each.
cmp_d0_source_maple: On GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 two years after each release.
cmp_d0_source_them: Closed. Dash0 open-sources its OpenTelemetry distribution and Kubernetes operator, not the platform.
cmp_d0_selfhost_maple: Yes. Run the whole platform on your own infrastructure, including your own ClickHouse.
cmp_d0_selfhost_them: No. SaaS only, in Dash0-operated regions.
cmp_d0_retention_maple: 30 days on the cloud plan, longer on Enterprise, and your call when you self-host.
cmp_d0_retention_them: 30 days for spans, logs and web events and 13 months for metrics, included in the storage rate.
cmp_d0_pricing_maple: $39 a month with 100 GB per signal included, then $0.30 per GB.
cmp_d0_pricing_them: Per data point: $0.60 per million spans or log records ($0.06 ingestion plus $0.54 storage at 30-day retention) and $0.20 per million metric data points ($0.02 plus $0.18 at 13-month retention).
cmp_d0_ai_maple: Built-in diagnostics plus a hosted MCP server.
cmp_d0_ai_them: An MCP server and AI-assisted views.
cmp_d0_promql_maple: No PromQL. Visual builder and SQL.
cmp_d0_promql_them: PromQL for metrics and Perses-based dashboards-as-code.
cmp_d0_k8s_tooling_maple: Kubernetes monitoring through the OpenTelemetry Collector. No operator of Maple's own.
cmp_d0_k8s_tooling_them: A Kubernetes operator and an OpenTelemetry distribution, both maintained in the open.
cmp_d0_mig_1_body: Both platforms ingest standard OTLP, so SDKs, auto-instrumentation and semantic conventions carry over unchanged.
cmp_d0_mig_2_body: Add Maple next to the Dash0 exporter in the Collector and ship to both while you verify.
cmp_d0_mig_3_body: Dashboards, saved views and alert rules don't travel over OTLP. Rebuild the ones that matter in Maple; the MCP server can draft them.
cmp_d0_faq_1_q: How is Maple different from Dash0?
cmp_d0_faq_1_a: The fundamentals match: both are OpenTelemetry-native, both price on usage with no per-seat fee for observability, both expose an MCP server. The difference is ownership. Maple is open source under FSL-1.1 and self-hostable on your own infrastructure with retention you control. Dash0 is a closed, SaaS-only backend.
cmp_d0_faq_2_q: Is Maple open source? Can I self-host it?
cmp_d0_faq_2_a: Yes to both. Maple's source is on GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0. Dash0 open-sources client-side tooling, its OpenTelemetry distribution and Kubernetes operator, but not the platform, and offers no self-hosting.
cmp_d0_faq_3_a: The pipeline is one exporter change: both platforms ingest standard OTLP. Dashboards, saved views and alert rules don't transfer, so plan to recreate those.
cmp_d0_faq_4_a: Both are usage-based with no per-seat fee for observability. Dash0 bills per data point; Maple bills per GB of decoded OTLP. Which is cheaper depends on how large your spans and log records are. The receipts above convert at one kilobyte per span or log record and 0.1 KB per metric data point; the calculator lets you change the counts.
cmp_d0_faq_5_q: Does Dash0 have anything Maple doesn't?
cmp_d0_faq_5_a: PromQL for metrics, Perses dashboards-as-code, synthetic API checks, and a vendor-maintained Kubernetes operator and OpenTelemetry distribution. Those rows are marked above.
cmp_sn_seo_title: Maple vs SigNoz: two OpenTelemetry-native, ClickHouse-backed platforms compared
cmp_sn_seo_desc: Maple vs SigNoz: both OpenTelemetry-native, ClickHouse-backed, one app for traces, logs and metrics. Where they differ (license, self-hosting, the error workflow, session replay, retention pricing), where SigNoz is ahead, and what one month costs on each.

Below: the rows where they diverge, where SigNoz is ahead, and what the same month costs on each.
cmp_sn_retention_maple: 30 days on every signal at the flat rate. Longer on Enterprise, and your call when you self-host.
cmp_sn_retention_them: 15 days for logs and traces and one month for metrics by default. Longer retention raises the per-GB and per-sample rates; the calculator on SigNoz's pricing page quotes them.
cmp_sn_pricing_maple: $39 a month with 100 GB per signal included, then $0.30 per GB. Metrics are metered by volume, not by sample.
cmp_sn_pricing_them: $49 a month including $49 of usage, then $0.30 per GB of logs and traces and $0.10 per million metric samples. Enterprise from $4,000 a month.
cmp_sn_errors_maple: Exceptions become issues with an owner, a state, a severity and comments. A resolved issue that fires again reopens.
cmp_sn_errors_them: An exceptions list grouped by service, type and message, each linked to its trace. No state, owner or severity on a group.
cmp_sn_rum_maple: Browser session replay with the trace behind every click. 5,000 sessions a month included.
cmp_sn_rum_them: Browser traces, logs and Web Vitals over OpenTelemetry. No session replay.
cmp_sn_local_maple: One binary with an embedded ClickHouse. `maple start` on a laptop, no containers, no account.
cmp_sn_local_them: The Linux install still needs ClickHouse and Postgres beside it; Docker wants 4 GB of memory.
cmp_sn_source_maple: FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 two years after each release. One license, no enterprise directory.
cmp_sn_source_them: MIT core, plus an `ee/` directory under a commercial license that holds SAML, OIDC and fine-grained RBAC.
cmp_sn_ai_maple: A hosted MCP server exposing the product's own queries, scoped to the org, with write tools for alert rules, dashboards and issues.
cmp_sn_ai_them: A hosted MCP server with fifty-plus tools, agent skills for Claude, Codex and Cursor, and Noz, an AI teammate that is Cloud-only.
cmp_sn_selfhost_maple: The repository, a compose file, your Postgres and ClickHouse, one root password. Single-org, no SSO yet.
cmp_sn_selfhost_them: Docker, Swarm, Helm and Foundry installs with per-platform guides. Multi-user with roles and Google OAuth in the Community edition.
cmp_sn_promql_maple: No PromQL. Visual builder and SQL, one grammar across signals.
cmp_sn_promql_them: Query Builder v5, ClickHouse SQL and PromQL in dashboards. Prometheus rules carry over.
cmp_sn_cost_controls_maple: Overage caps per signal and usage alerts in the billing settings. At a cap the ingest gateway rejects that signal until the billing cycle resets.
cmp_sn_cost_controls_them: Ingest Guard: daily caps per signal and per team in Cloud that drop data past the limit.
cmp_sn_channels_maple: Slack, PagerDuty, Discord, Telegram, email and webhooks.
cmp_sn_channels_them: Nine channel types, including Opsgenie, Microsoft Teams, Incident.io, Rootly and Zenduty.
cmp_sn_mig_1_title: Keep the Collector, add an exporter
cmp_sn_mig_1_body: Both platforms ingest standard OTLP, so SDKs, auto-instrumentation and semantic conventions carry over unchanged. Add Maple next to the SigNoz exporter and ship to both until the alerts you care about fire from Maple.
cmp_sn_mig_2_title: Move the dashboards and alerts with one prompt
cmp_sn_mig_2_body: Dashboards and alert rules don't travel over OTLP, but both MCP servers expose them: SigNoz's reads them, Maple's creates them. Connect an agent to both and ask it to port everything. One prompt is usually enough, PromQL panels included.
cmp_sn_faq_1_a: The core is MIT. The `ee/` directory is under the SigNoz Enterprise License, which forbids production use without a paid license, and currently holds SAML and OIDC single sign-on and fine-grained RBAC. Maple is under FSL-1.1, source-available for two years per release and Apache 2.0 after, with no enterprise-only directory.
cmp_sn_faq_2_q: How is Maple different from SigNoz?
cmp_sn_faq_2_a: The bones match: OpenTelemetry in, ClickHouse underneath, one app, usage pricing, an MCP server. Maple keeps going after the error is found, with issues that have an owner and a state, browser session replay, agent sessions for AI workloads, and a single-binary local mode. SigNoz is ahead on self-hosting maturity and PromQL.
cmp_sn_faq_3_q: Which is cheaper, SigNoz or Maple?
cmp_sn_faq_3_a: At small volumes they are within ten dollars of each other: $49 against $39. Above that, Maple includes 100 GB per signal and keeps 30 days at the same rate, while SigNoz's rate rises with retention. SigNoz's per-sample metric pricing can win if your metrics are many and small. The receipts above run both models on the same month.
cmp_sn_faq_4_a: Yes. SigNoz has the more polished path today: Docker Compose, Helm, Foundry and platform guides, multi-user with roles in the Community edition. Maple self-hosts from the repository with a compose file, your ClickHouse and a root password, single-org, and runs as one binary with an embedded ClickHouse for local development.
cmp_sn_faq_5_a: No. SigNoz ingests browser traces, logs and Web Vitals over OpenTelemetry. Maple records and replays browser sessions with the trace behind each event, masked in the browser before anything leaves the page.
cmp_ax_seo_title: Maple vs Axiom: an event store with APL, or a platform you can self-host
cmp_ax_seo_desc: Maple vs Axiom: both ingest OpenTelemetry and bill on usage with no per-seat fee. Where they differ on price, the error workflow, session replay, self-hosting and APL. Where Axiom is ahead, and what one month costs on each.
cmp_ax_hero_lede: Axiom and Maple both take OpenTelemetry in, bill on usage, and charge nothing per seat. The difference is what sits on top of the store. Axiom gives you APL and a dashboard builder. Maple ships the surfaces built, including the service map, session replay and web analytics, and you can self-host all of it. Below: where the two diverge, what Axiom leaves you to build, where Axiom is ahead, and what the same month costs on each.
cmp_ax_pricing_maple: $39 a month with 100 GB per signal included, then $0.30 per GB. Browser sessions are the only other meter. Queries and storage are not separate line items.
cmp_ax_pricing_them: $25 a month, then three meters: data loading from $0.12 per GB, query compute from $0.20 per GB-hour, storage $0.03 per GB. The free allowance is 1 TB, 100 GB-hours and 100 GB. Single sign-on costs $100 a month, RBAC and the audit log $50 each.
cmp_ax_volume_pricing_maple: $0.30 per GB at every volume. Lower rates exist on Enterprise but are not published.
cmp_ax_volume_pricing_them: The ingest rate falls as volume grows, with no negotiation: $0.12 per GB, $0.085 above 500 TB, $0.06 above 5 PB. Pre-purchased credits on a 12- to 36-month term take a further discount.
cmp_ax_errors_maple: Exceptions become issues with an owner, a state, a severity and comments. A resolved issue that fires again reopens.
cmp_ax_errors_them: No issue object. Exceptions stay events: you query them in APL, group by message, and have a monitor notify per group.
cmp_ax_rum_maple: Browser session replay with the trace behind every click, web analytics from the browser SDK, and a Swift SDK for iOS.
cmp_ax_rum_them: Web Vitals from the browser and a zero-config app for Vercel. No session replay, no mobile SDK.
cmp_ax_local_maple: One binary with an embedded ClickHouse. `maple start` on a laptop, no containers, no account.
cmp_ax_local_them: Cloud only. Local work still means a dataset in a real organization and a token in your environment.
cmp_ax_source_maple: On GitHub under FSL-1.1, converting to Apache 2.0 two years after each release.
cmp_ax_source_them: Closed. The SDKs, Collector configurations and the Vercel app are public. The platform is not.
cmp_ax_selfhost_maple: Yes. The whole platform on your own infrastructure, your own ClickHouse, retention you set.
cmp_ax_selfhost_them: No. Axiom runs the edge deployments, in US East and EU Central. Enterprise can point storage at its own S3 bucket.
cmp_ax_retention_maple: 30 days on the cloud plan at the flat rate. Longer on Enterprise, and your call when you self-host.
cmp_ax_retention_them: Configurable per dataset and billed as storage: $0.03 per compressed GB a month for the first 60 days, $0.0163 to 120 days and $0.0052 after that, with 100 GB free.
cmp_ax_query_maple: One visual builder across every signal. When you want the query itself it is ClickHouse SQL, through the API or the MCP server.
cmp_ax_query_them: APL for events, MPL for metrics. Over a hundred functions, plus a skill that translates Splunk's SPL into APL.
cmp_ax_ai_maple: A hosted MCP server over the product's own queries, scoped to the org. Investigations run the diagnosis and write up what broke.
cmp_ax_ai_them: An MCP server, six agent skills (SRE, metrics, dashboards, alerting, cost control, SPL translation) and Spotlight, which diffs two sets of events. Query cost limits per token stop an agent running up the bill.
cmp_ax_integrations_maple: OpenTelemetry receivers plus a catalog of connected providers: Cloudflare, Prometheus, PlanetScale, WarpStream, Hazel and GitHub. Kubernetes and Docker are agent installs.
cmp_ax_integrations_them: Over forty apps, including Vector, CloudWatch, Lambda, Heroku and CI/CD. A Splunk app federates search across both tools.
cmp_ax_cost_controls_maple: Overage caps per signal and usage alerts in the billing settings. At a cap the ingest gateway rejects that signal until the billing cycle resets.
cmp_ax_cost_controls_them: Spend alerts and hard caps in the console. Past the limit, ingestion pauses instead of billing as overage.
cmp_ax_compliance_maple: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification in progress. Maple Cloud runs in the US or the EU (Frankfurt) at the same price, and self-hosting keeps the data in your own audited environment.
cmp_ax_compliance_them: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR, a self-serve HIPAA BAA, and a choice of US or EU residency.
cmp_ax_mig_1_title: Keep the Collector, add an exporter
cmp_ax_mig_1_body: Both platforms ingest standard OTLP, so SDKs, auto-instrumentation and semantic conventions carry over unchanged. Add Maple next to the Axiom exporter and ship to both until the alerts you care about fire from Maple.
cmp_ax_mig_2_title: Move the dashboards and monitors with one prompt
cmp_ax_mig_2_body: Dashboards and monitors do not travel over OTLP, and neither does APL. Both platforms expose an MCP server: Axiom's reads what you have, Maple's creates it. Connect an agent to both and ask it to port everything, translating the queries as it goes.
cmp_ax_faq_1_q: Is Axiom open source? Can I self-host it?
cmp_ax_faq_1_a: No to both. Axiom publishes its SDKs, Collector configurations and the Vercel app, but the platform is closed and runs only in Axiom's own edge deployments, today US East and EU Central. Enterprise customers can keep object storage in their own S3 bucket, which is data residency rather than self-hosting. Maple's source is on GitHub under FSL-1.1, converts to Apache 2.0 two years after each release, and runs on your own infrastructure with your own ClickHouse.
cmp_ax_faq_2_q: How is Maple different from Axiom?
cmp_ax_faq_2_a: Axiom is an event store first. Everything lands in a dataset, you query it in APL, and a monitor runs that query on a schedule. Maple is the product on top of that storage. Exceptions become issues with an owner and a state, browser sessions replay with the trace behind each click, agent sessions are a signal of their own, and one binary runs the whole thing on a laptop. Axiom is ahead on price at volume, retention economics, integration breadth and compliance.
cmp_ax_faq_3_q: Which is cheaper, Axiom or Maple?
cmp_ax_faq_3_a: At the reference workload Maple is, because Axiom's platform fee and query-compute meter start charging before Maple's overage does. Above a terabyte a month Axiom's ingest rate is the lower one and keeps falling with volume, and its storage pricing makes long retention cheap. The receipts above run both published rate cards on the same month, and the calculator lets you change the volumes.
cmp_ax_faq_4_q: Does Axiom have error tracking or session replay?
cmp_ax_faq_4_a: Not as products. Exceptions are events you query in APL and group inside a monitor, so nothing carries an owner, a state or a reopen. There is no session replay. Maple has both: issues with a lifecycle, and browser replay masked in the page before anything leaves it.
cmp_ax_faq_5_q: Do I have to learn APL?
cmp_ax_faq_5_a: On Axiom, mostly yes. APL for events, MPL for metrics, and a skill that translates SPL if you are arriving from Splunk. Maple's visual builder covers every signal, and when you want the query itself it is ClickHouse SQL, through the API or the MCP server.
cmp_ax_surfaces_lede: Axiom stores events and hands you a dashboard builder. Every view is a panel you write in APL. Maple ships these four built, and none of them is a chart you could assemble out of panels.
cmp_ax_surface_map_instead: no dependency graph. You aggregate caller and callee pairs in APL and read the topology as a table.
cmp_ax_surface_sessions_instead: nothing to build on. Axiom stores browser events if you send them, but there is no capture and no replay.
cmp_ax_surface_analytics_instead: a dashboard you assemble from APL over your own events, with no path from a number to the session that produced it.
cmp_ax_surface_k8s_instead: a Kubernetes app that ships the data, and dashboards you build over it.
home_objection_selfhost_detail: Every line of Maple's source is on GitHub under FSL-1.1, and each release becomes Apache 2.0 after two years. Run it on your own infrastructure with no license call.
home_objection_otel_detail: Maple speaks plain OpenTelemetry. Point an OTLP exporter at it and keep the instrumentation you already wrote. If you leave, there is nothing to rip out.
home_objection_trial_detail: A card is required to start the trial and nothing is charged until it ends. No per-seat, per-host or per-query fees at any volume.
home_objection_region_claim: Hosted in the US or the EU
home_objection_region_detail: Choose the EU when you sign up and your telemetry is stored and processed in Frankfurt. Same plan and price in both regions.
faq_region_a: Maple Cloud runs in two regions: the United States and the European Union (Frankfurt, Germany). You choose one when you create your organization, and all of its telemetry is stored and processed there. The region cannot be changed later. Pricing is the same in both. To keep the data inside your own network, self-host Maple.
pricing_regions_note: Hosted in the US or the EU (Frankfurt) at the same price.
pricing_region_claim: Hosted in the US or the EU
pricing_region_same_body: Pick a region when you create your organization. Its telemetry is stored and processed there. AI chat is not available in the EU region yet.
